# nutype/lib.rs

[1](https://docs.rs#1)//! <p align="center"><img width="300" src="https://raw.githubusercontent.com/greyblake/nutype/master/art/rust_nutype.png" alt="Rust Nutype Logo"></p>
[2](https://docs.rs#2)//! <h2 align="center">The newtype with guarantees.</h2>
[3](https://docs.rs#3)//!
[4](https://docs.rs#4)//! Nutype is a proc macro that allows adding extra constraints like _sanitization_ and _validation_ to the regular [newtype pattern](https://doc.rust-lang.org/rust-by-example/generics/new_types.html). The generated code makes it impossible to instantiate a value without passing the checks. It works this way even with `serde` deserialization.
[5](https://docs.rs#5)//!
[6](https://docs.rs#6)//!
[7](https://docs.rs#7)//! ## Quick start
[8](https://docs.rs#8)//!
[9](https://docs.rs#9)//! ```
[10](https://docs.rs#10)//! use nutype::nutype;
[11](https://docs.rs#11)//!
[12](https://docs.rs#12)//! #[nutype(
[13](https://docs.rs#13)//!     sanitize(trim, lowercase),
[14](https://docs.rs#14)//!     validate(not_empty, len_char_max = 20),
[15](https://docs.rs#15)//!     derive(Debug, PartialEq),
[16](https://docs.rs#16)//! )]
[17](https://docs.rs#17)//! pub struct Username(String);
[18](https://docs.rs#18)//!
[19](https://docs.rs#19)//! // Now we can create usernames:
[20](https://docs.rs#20)//! assert_eq!(
[21](https://docs.rs#21)//!     Username::try_new("   FooBar  ").unwrap().into_inner(),
[22](https://docs.rs#22)//!     "foobar"
[23](https://docs.rs#23)//! );
[24](https://docs.rs#24)//!
[25](https://docs.rs#25)//! // But we cannot create invalid ones:
[26](https://docs.rs#26)//! assert_eq!(
[27](https://docs.rs#27)//!     Username::try_new("   "),
[28](https://docs.rs#28)//!     Err(UsernameError::NotEmptyViolated),
[29](https://docs.rs#29)//! );
[30](https://docs.rs#30)//!
[31](https://docs.rs#31)//! assert_eq!(
[32](https://docs.rs#32)//!     Username::try_new("TheUserNameIsVeryVeryLong"),
[33](https://docs.rs#33)//!     Err(UsernameError::LenCharMaxViolated),
[34](https://docs.rs#34)//! );
[35](https://docs.rs#35)//! ```
[36](https://docs.rs#36)//!
[37](https://docs.rs#37)//! Note, that we also got `UsernameError` enum generated implicitly.
[38](https://docs.rs#38)//!
[39](https://docs.rs#39)//! Ok, but let's try to obtain an instance of `Username` that violates the validation rules:
[40](https://docs.rs#40)//!
[41](https://docs.rs#41)//! ```compile_fail
[42](https://docs.rs#42)//! use nutype::nutype;
[43](https://docs.rs#43)//!
[44](https://docs.rs#44)//! #[nutype(validate(not_empty))]
[45](https://docs.rs#45)//! pub struct Username(String);
[46](https://docs.rs#46)//!
[47](https://docs.rs#47)//! // error[E0423]: cannot initialize a tuple struct which contains private fields
[48](https://docs.rs#48)//! let username = Username("".to_string());
[49](https://docs.rs#49)//! ```
[50](https://docs.rs#50)//!
[51](https://docs.rs#51)//! ```compile_fail
[52](https://docs.rs#52)//! use nutype::nutype;
[53](https://docs.rs#53)//!
[54](https://docs.rs#54)//! #[nutype(validate(not_empty))]
[55](https://docs.rs#55)//! pub struct Username(String);
[56](https://docs.rs#56)//!
[57](https://docs.rs#57)//! let mut username = Username::try_new("foo").unwrap();
[58](https://docs.rs#58)//! // error[E0616]: field `0` of struct `Username` is private
[59](https://docs.rs#59)//! username.0 = "".to_string();
[60](https://docs.rs#60)//! ```
[61](https://docs.rs#61)//!
[62](https://docs.rs#62)//! Haha. It does not seem to be easy!
[63](https://docs.rs#63)//!
[64](https://docs.rs#64)//!
[65](https://docs.rs#65)//! ## A few more examples
[66](https://docs.rs#66)//!
[67](https://docs.rs#67)//! Here are some other examples of what you can do with `nutype`.
[68](https://docs.rs#68)//!
[69](https://docs.rs#69)//! You can skip `sanitize` and use a custom validator `predicate`:
[70](https://docs.rs#70)//!
[71](https://docs.rs#71)//! ```
[72](https://docs.rs#72)//! use nutype::nutype;
[73](https://docs.rs#73)//!
[74](https://docs.rs#74)//! #[nutype(validate(predicate = |n| n % 2 == 1))]
[75](https://docs.rs#75)//! struct OddNumber(i64);
[76](https://docs.rs#76)//! ```
[77](https://docs.rs#77)//!
[78](https://docs.rs#78)//! You can skip validation, if you need sanitization only:
[79](https://docs.rs#79)//!
[80](https://docs.rs#80)//! ```
[81](https://docs.rs#81)//! use nutype::nutype;
[82](https://docs.rs#82)//!
[83](https://docs.rs#83)//! #[nutype(sanitize(trim, lowercase))]
[84](https://docs.rs#84)//! struct Username(String);
[85](https://docs.rs#85)//! ```
[86](https://docs.rs#86)//!
[87](https://docs.rs#87)//! In that case, `Username::new(String)` simply returns `Username`, not `Result`.
[88](https://docs.rs#88)//!
[89](https://docs.rs#89)//!
[90](https://docs.rs#90)//! ## Inner types
[91](https://docs.rs#91)//!
[92](https://docs.rs#92)//! Available sanitizers, validators, and derivable traits are determined by the inner type, which falls into the following categories:
[93](https://docs.rs#93)//! * String
[94](https://docs.rs#94)//! * Integer (`u8`, `u16`,`u32`, `u64`, `u128`, `i8`, `i16`, `i32`, `i64`, `i128`, `usize`, `isize`)
[95](https://docs.rs#95)//! * Float (`f32`, `f64`)
[96](https://docs.rs#96)//! * Any other arbitrary type
[97](https://docs.rs#97)//!
[98](https://docs.rs#98)//! ## String
[99](https://docs.rs#99)//!
[100](https://docs.rs#100)//! At the moment the string inner type supports only `String` (owned) type.
[101](https://docs.rs#101)//!
[102](https://docs.rs#102)//! ### String sanitizers
[103](https://docs.rs#103)//!
[104](https://docs.rs#104)//! | Sanitizer   | Description                                                                         | Example                                         |
[105](https://docs.rs#105)//! |-------------|-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|-------------------------------------------------|
[106](https://docs.rs#106)//! | `trim`      | Removes leading and trailing whitespaces                                            | `trim`                                          |
[107](https://docs.rs#107)//! | `lowercase` | Converts the string to lowercase                                                    | `lowercase`                                     |
[108](https://docs.rs#108)//! | `uppercase` | Converts the string to uppercase                                                    | `uppercase`                                     |
[109](https://docs.rs#109)//! | `with`      | Custom sanitizer. A function or closure that receives `String` and returns `String` | `with = \|mut s: String\| { s.truncate(5); s }` |
[110](https://docs.rs#110)//!
[111](https://docs.rs#111)//! ### String validators
[112](https://docs.rs#112)//!
[113](https://docs.rs#113)//! | Validator       | Description                                                                     | Error variant         | Example                                      |
[114](https://docs.rs#114)//! |-----------------|---------------------------------------------------------------------------------|-----------------------|----------------------------------------------|
[115](https://docs.rs#115)//! | `len_char_min`  | Min length of the string (in chars, not bytes)                                  | `LenCharMinViolated`  | `len_char_min = 5`                           |
[116](https://docs.rs#116)//! | `len_char_max`  | Max length of the string (in chars, not bytes)                                  | `LenCharMaxViolated`  | `len_char_max = 255`                         |
[117](https://docs.rs#117)//! | `len_utf16_min` | Min length of the string in UTF-16 code units (useful for JavaScript interop)   | `LenUtf16MinViolated` | `len_utf16_min = 5`                          |
[118](https://docs.rs#118)//! | `len_utf16_max` | Max length of the string in UTF-16 code units (useful for JavaScript interop)   | `LenUtf16MaxViolated` | `len_utf16_max = 255`                        |
[119](https://docs.rs#119)//! | `not_empty`     | Rejects an empty string                                                         | `NotEmptyViolated`    | `not_empty`                                  |
[120](https://docs.rs#120)//! | `regex`         | Validates format with a regex. Requires `regex` feature.                        | `RegexViolated`       | `regex = "^[0-9]{7}$"` or `regex = ID_REGEX` |
[121](https://docs.rs#121)//! | `predicate`     | Custom validator. A function or closure that receives `&str` and returns `bool` | `PredicateViolated`   | `predicate = \|s: &str\| s.contains('@')`    |
[122](https://docs.rs#122)//! | `with`          | Custom validator with a custom error                                            | N/A                   | (see example below)                          |
[123](https://docs.rs#123)//!
[124](https://docs.rs#124)//! #### Regex validation
[125](https://docs.rs#125)//!
[126](https://docs.rs#126)//! Requirements:
[127](https://docs.rs#127)//! * `regex` feature of `nutype` is enabled.
[128](https://docs.rs#128)//! * You crate have to explicitly include `regex` as a dependency.
[129](https://docs.rs#129)//!
[130](https://docs.rs#130)//! There are a number of ways you can use regex.
[131](https://docs.rs#131)//!
[132](https://docs.rs#132)//! A regular expression can be defined right in place:
[133](https://docs.rs#133)//!
[134](https://docs.rs#134)//! ```
[135](https://docs.rs#135)//! # mod wrapper_module {
[136](https://docs.rs#136)//!
[137](https://docs.rs#137)//! use nutype::nutype;
[138](https://docs.rs#138)//!
[139](https://docs.rs#139)//! #[nutype(validate(regex = "^[0-9]{3}-[0-9]{3}$"))]
[140](https://docs.rs#140)//! pub struct PhoneNumber(String);
[141](https://docs.rs#141)//!
[142](https://docs.rs#142)//! # }
[143](https://docs.rs#143)//! ```
[144](https://docs.rs#144)//!
[145](https://docs.rs#145)//! or it can be defined with `std::sync::LazyLock`:
[146](https://docs.rs#146)//!
[147](https://docs.rs#147)//! ```
[148](https://docs.rs#148)//! # mod wrapper_module {
[149](https://docs.rs#149)//!
[150](https://docs.rs#150)//! use nutype::nutype;
[151](https://docs.rs#151)//! use std::sync::LazyLock;
[152](https://docs.rs#152)//! use regex::Regex;
[153](https://docs.rs#153)//!
[154](https://docs.rs#154)//! static PHONE_NUMBER_REGEX: LazyLock<Regex> = LazyLock::new(|| Regex::new("^[0-9]{3}-[0-9]{3}$").unwrap());
[155](https://docs.rs#155)//!
[156](https://docs.rs#156)//! #[nutype(validate(regex = PHONE_NUMBER_REGEX))]
[157](https://docs.rs#157)//! pub struct PhoneNumber(String);
[158](https://docs.rs#158)//!
[159](https://docs.rs#159)//! # }
[160](https://docs.rs#160)//! ```
[161](https://docs.rs#161)//!
[162](https://docs.rs#162)//! or it can be defined with `lazy_static`:
[163](https://docs.rs#163)//!
[164](https://docs.rs#164)//! ```
[165](https://docs.rs#165)//! # mod wrapper_module {
[166](https://docs.rs#166)//!
[167](https://docs.rs#167)//! use nutype::nutype;
[168](https://docs.rs#168)//! use lazy_static::lazy_static;
[169](https://docs.rs#169)//! use regex::Regex;
[170](https://docs.rs#170)//!
[171](https://docs.rs#171)//! lazy_static! {
[172](https://docs.rs#172)//!     static ref PHONE_NUMBER_REGEX: Regex = Regex::new("^[0-9]{3}-[0-9]{3}$").unwrap();
[173](https://docs.rs#173)//! }
[174](https://docs.rs#174)//!
[175](https://docs.rs#175)//! #[nutype(validate(regex = PHONE_NUMBER_REGEX))]
[176](https://docs.rs#176)//! pub struct PhoneNumber(String);
[177](https://docs.rs#177)//!
[178](https://docs.rs#178)//! # }
[179](https://docs.rs#179)//! ```
[180](https://docs.rs#180)//!
[181](https://docs.rs#181)//! or `once_cell`:
[182](https://docs.rs#182)//!
[183](https://docs.rs#183)//! ```
[184](https://docs.rs#184)//! # mod wrapper_module {
[185](https://docs.rs#185)//!
[186](https://docs.rs#186)//! use nutype::nutype;
[187](https://docs.rs#187)//! use once_cell::sync::Lazy;
[188](https://docs.rs#188)//! use regex::Regex;
[189](https://docs.rs#189)//!
[190](https://docs.rs#190)//! static PHONE_NUMBER_REGEX: Lazy<Regex> =
[191](https://docs.rs#191)//!     Lazy::new(|| Regex::new("[0-9]{3}-[0-9]{3}$").unwrap());
[192](https://docs.rs#192)//!
[193](https://docs.rs#193)//! #[nutype(validate(regex = PHONE_NUMBER_REGEX))]
[194](https://docs.rs#194)//! pub struct PhoneNumber(String);
[195](https://docs.rs#195)//!
[196](https://docs.rs#196)//! # }
[197](https://docs.rs#197)//! ```
[198](https://docs.rs#198)//!
[199](https://docs.rs#199)//!
[200](https://docs.rs#200)//! ### String derivable traits
[201](https://docs.rs#201)//!
[202](https://docs.rs#202)//! The following traits can be derived for a string-based type:
[203](https://docs.rs#203)//! `Debug`, `Clone`, `PartialEq`, `Eq`, `PartialOrd`, `Ord`, `FromStr`, `AsRef`, `Deref`,
[204](https://docs.rs#204)//! `From`, `TryFrom`, `Into`, `Hash`, `Borrow`, `Display`, `Default`, `Serialize`, `Deserialize`.
[205](https://docs.rs#205)//!
[206](https://docs.rs#206)//!
[207](https://docs.rs#207)//! ## Integer
[208](https://docs.rs#208)//!
[209](https://docs.rs#209)//! The integer inner types are: `u8`, `u16`,`u32`, `u64`, `u128`, `i8`, `i16`, `i32`, `i64`, `i128`, `usize`, `isize`.
[210](https://docs.rs#210)//!
[211](https://docs.rs#211)//! ### Integer sanitizers
[212](https://docs.rs#212)//!
[213](https://docs.rs#213)//! | Sanitizer | Description       | Example                            |
[214](https://docs.rs#214)//! |-----------|-------------------|------------------------------------|
[215](https://docs.rs#215)//! | `with`    | Custom sanitizer. | `with = \|raw\| raw.clamp(0, 100)` |
[216](https://docs.rs#216)//!
[217](https://docs.rs#217)//! ### Integer validators
[218](https://docs.rs#218)//!
[219](https://docs.rs#219)//! | Validator           | Description                           | Error variant             | Example                              |
[220](https://docs.rs#220)//! | ------------------- | ------------------------------------- | ------------------------- | ------------------------------------ |
[221](https://docs.rs#221)//! | `less`              | Exclusive upper bound                 | `LessViolated`            | `less = 100`                         |
[222](https://docs.rs#222)//! | `less_or_equal`     | Inclusive upper bound                 | `LessOrEqualViolated`     | `less_or_equal = 99`                 |
[223](https://docs.rs#223)//! | `greater`           | Exclusive lower bound                 | `GreaterViolated`         | `greater = 17`                       |
[224](https://docs.rs#224)//! | `greater_or_equal`  | Inclusive lower bound                 | `GreaterOrEqualViolated`  | `greater_or_equal = 18`              |
[225](https://docs.rs#225)//! | `predicate`         | Custom predicate                      | `PredicateViolated`       | `predicate = \|num\| num % 2 == 0`   |
[226](https://docs.rs#226)//! | `with`              | Custom validator with a custom error  | N/A                       | (see example below)                  |
[227](https://docs.rs#227)//!
[228](https://docs.rs#228)//! ### Integer derivable traits
[229](https://docs.rs#229)//!
[230](https://docs.rs#230)//! The following traits can be derived for an integer-based type:
[231](https://docs.rs#231)//! `Debug`, `Clone`, `Copy`, `PartialEq`, `Eq`, `PartialOrd`, `Ord`, `FromStr`, `AsRef`, `Deref`,
[232](https://docs.rs#232)//! `Into`, `From`, `TryFrom`, `Hash`, `Borrow`, `Display`, `Default`, `Serialize`, `Deserialize`.
[233](https://docs.rs#233)//!
[234](https://docs.rs#234)//!
[235](https://docs.rs#235)//! ## Float
[236](https://docs.rs#236)//!
[237](https://docs.rs#237)//! The float inner types are: `f32`, `f64`.
[238](https://docs.rs#238)//!
[239](https://docs.rs#239)//! ### Float sanitizers
[240](https://docs.rs#240)//!
[241](https://docs.rs#241)//! | Sanitizer | Description       | Example                                |
[242](https://docs.rs#242)//! |-----------|-------------------|----------------------------------------|
[243](https://docs.rs#243)//! | `with`    | Custom sanitizer. | `with = \|val\| val.clamp(0.0, 100.0)` |
[244](https://docs.rs#244)//!
[245](https://docs.rs#245)//! ### Float validators
[246](https://docs.rs#246)//!
[247](https://docs.rs#247)//! | Validator          | Description                          | Error variant            | Example                             |
[248](https://docs.rs#248)//! | ------------------ | ------------------------------------ | ---------------------    | ----------------------------------- |
[249](https://docs.rs#249)//! | `less`             | Exclusive upper bound                | `LessViolated`           | `less = 100.0`                      |
[250](https://docs.rs#250)//! | `less_or_equal`    | Inclusive upper bound                | `LessOrEqualViolated`    | `less_or_equal = 100.0`             |
[251](https://docs.rs#251)//! | `greater`          | Exclusive lower bound                | `GreaterViolated`        | `greater = 0.0`                     |
[252](https://docs.rs#252)//! | `greater_or_equal` | Inclusive lower bound                | `GreaterOrEqualViolated` | `greater_or_equal = 0.0`            |
[253](https://docs.rs#253)//! | `finite`           | Check against NaN and infinity       | `FiniteViolated`         | `finite`                            |
[254](https://docs.rs#254)//! | `predicate`        | Custom predicate                     | `PredicateViolated`      | `predicate = \|val\| val != 50.0`   |
[255](https://docs.rs#255)//! | `with`             | Custom validator with a custom error | N/A                      | (see example below)                 |
[256](https://docs.rs#256)//!
[257](https://docs.rs#257)//! ### Float derivable traits
[258](https://docs.rs#258)//!
[259](https://docs.rs#259)//! The following traits can be derived for a float-based type:
[260](https://docs.rs#260)//! `Debug`, `Clone`, `Copy`, `PartialEq`, `Eq`, `PartialOrd`, `Ord`, `FromStr`, `AsRef`, `Deref`,
[261](https://docs.rs#261)//! `Into`, `From`, `TryFrom`, `Hash`, `Borrow`, `Display`, `Default`, `Serialize`, `Deserialize`.
[262](https://docs.rs#262)//!
[263](https://docs.rs#263)//! It's also possible to derive `Eq` and `Ord` if the validation rules guarantee that `NaN` is excluded.
[264](https://docs.rs#264)//! This can be done by applying `finite` validation. For example:
[265](https://docs.rs#265)//!
[266](https://docs.rs#266)//! ```rust
[267](https://docs.rs#267)//! use nutype::nutype;
[268](https://docs.rs#268)//!
[269](https://docs.rs#269)//! #[nutype(
[270](https://docs.rs#270)//!     validate(finite),
[271](https://docs.rs#271)//!     derive(PartialEq, Eq, PartialOrd, Ord),
[272](https://docs.rs#272)//! )]
[273](https://docs.rs#273)//! struct Size(f64);
[274](https://docs.rs#274)//! ```
[275](https://docs.rs#275)//!
[276](https://docs.rs#276)//! ## Other inner types and generics
[277](https://docs.rs#277)//!
[278](https://docs.rs#278)//! For any other type it is possible to define custom sanitizers with `with` and custom
[279](https://docs.rs#279)//! validations with `predicate` or `with`:
[280](https://docs.rs#280)//!
[281](https://docs.rs#281)//! ```
[282](https://docs.rs#282)//! use nutype::nutype;
[283](https://docs.rs#283)//!
[284](https://docs.rs#284)//! #[nutype(
[285](https://docs.rs#285)//!     derive(Debug, PartialEq, AsRef, Deref),
[286](https://docs.rs#286)//!     sanitize(with = |mut guests| { guests.sort(); guests }),
[287](https://docs.rs#287)//!     validate(predicate = |guests| !guests.is_empty() ),
[288](https://docs.rs#288)//! )]
[289](https://docs.rs#289)//! pub struct GuestList(Vec<String>);
[290](https://docs.rs#290)//!
[291](https://docs.rs#291)//! ```
[292](https://docs.rs#292)//!
[293](https://docs.rs#293)//! It's also possible to use generics:
[294](https://docs.rs#294)//!
[295](https://docs.rs#295)//! ```
[296](https://docs.rs#296)//! use nutype::nutype;
[297](https://docs.rs#297)//!
[298](https://docs.rs#298)//! #[nutype(
[299](https://docs.rs#299)//!     sanitize(with = |mut v| { v.sort(); v }),
[300](https://docs.rs#300)//!     validate(predicate = |vec| !vec.is_empty()),
[301](https://docs.rs#301)//!     derive(Debug, PartialEq, AsRef, Deref),
[302](https://docs.rs#302)//! )]
[303](https://docs.rs#303)//! struct SortedNotEmptyVec<T: Ord>(Vec<T>);
[304](https://docs.rs#304)//!
[305](https://docs.rs#305)//! let wise_friends = SortedNotEmptyVec::try_new(vec!["Seneca", "Zeno", "Plato"]).unwrap();
[306](https://docs.rs#306)//! assert_eq!(wise_friends.as_ref(), &["Plato", "Seneca", "Zeno"]);
[307](https://docs.rs#307)//! assert_eq!(wise_friends.len(), 3);
[308](https://docs.rs#308)//!
[309](https://docs.rs#309)//! let numbers = SortedNotEmptyVec::try_new(vec![4, 2, 7, 1]).unwrap();
[310](https://docs.rs#310)//! assert_eq!(numbers.as_ref(), &[1, 2, 4, 7]);
[311](https://docs.rs#311)//! assert_eq!(numbers.len(), 4);
[312](https://docs.rs#312)//! ```
[313](https://docs.rs#313)//!
[314](https://docs.rs#314)//! ### Where clauses
[315](https://docs.rs#315)//!
[316](https://docs.rs#316)//! Nutype fully supports `where` clauses in generic newtypes, including Higher-Ranked Trait Bounds (HRTB):
[317](https://docs.rs#317)//!
[318](https://docs.rs#318)//! ```
[319](https://docs.rs#319)//! use nutype::nutype;
[320](https://docs.rs#320)//!
[321](https://docs.rs#321)//! // Simple where clause
[322](https://docs.rs#322)//! #[nutype(derive(Debug, Clone))]
[323](https://docs.rs#323)//! struct Wrapper<T>(T)
[324](https://docs.rs#324)//! where
[325](https://docs.rs#325)//!     T: Default + Clone;
[326](https://docs.rs#326)//!
[327](https://docs.rs#327)//! // HRTB for collections - validate that collection is non-empty
[328](https://docs.rs#328)//! #[nutype(
[329](https://docs.rs#329)//!     validate(predicate = |c| c.into_iter().next().is_some()),
[330](https://docs.rs#330)//!     derive(Debug)
[331](https://docs.rs#331)//! )]
[332](https://docs.rs#332)//! struct NonEmpty<C>(C)
[333](https://docs.rs#333)//! where
[334](https://docs.rs#334)//!     for<'a> &'a C: IntoIterator;
[335](https://docs.rs#335)//!
[336](https://docs.rs#336)//! // Usage
[337](https://docs.rs#337)//! let non_empty = NonEmpty::try_new(vec![1, 2, 3]).unwrap();
[338](https://docs.rs#338)//! assert!(NonEmpty::try_new(Vec::<i32>::new()).is_err());
[339](https://docs.rs#339)//! ```
[340](https://docs.rs#340)//!
[341](https://docs.rs#341)//! ## Custom sanitizers
[342](https://docs.rs#342)//!
[343](https://docs.rs#343)//! You can set custom sanitizers using the `with` option.
[344](https://docs.rs#344)//! A custom sanitizer is a function or closure that receives a value of an inner type with ownership and returns a sanitized value back.
[345](https://docs.rs#345)//!
[346](https://docs.rs#346)//! For example, this one
[347](https://docs.rs#347)//!
[348](https://docs.rs#348)//! ```
[349](https://docs.rs#349)//! # mod wrapper {
[350](https://docs.rs#350)//!
[351](https://docs.rs#351)//! use nutype::nutype;
[352](https://docs.rs#352)//!
[353](https://docs.rs#353)//! fn new_to_old(s: String) -> String {
[354](https://docs.rs#354)//!     s.replace("New", "Old")
[355](https://docs.rs#355)//! }
[356](https://docs.rs#356)//!
[357](https://docs.rs#357)//! #[nutype(sanitize(with = new_to_old))]
[358](https://docs.rs#358)//! struct CityName(String);
[359](https://docs.rs#359)//!
[360](https://docs.rs#360)//! # }
[361](https://docs.rs#361)//! ```
[362](https://docs.rs#362)//!
[363](https://docs.rs#363)//! is equal to the following one:
[364](https://docs.rs#364)//!
[365](https://docs.rs#365)//! ```
[366](https://docs.rs#366)//! use nutype::nutype;
[367](https://docs.rs#367)//!
[368](https://docs.rs#368)//! #[nutype(sanitize(with = |s| s.replace("New", "Old") ))]
[369](https://docs.rs#369)//! struct CityName(String);
[370](https://docs.rs#370)//!
[371](https://docs.rs#371)//! // And works the same way:
[372](https://docs.rs#372)//! let city = CityName::new("New York");
[373](https://docs.rs#373)//! assert_eq!(city.into_inner(), "Old York");
[374](https://docs.rs#374)//! ```
[375](https://docs.rs#375)//!
[376](https://docs.rs#376)//! ## Custom validation with predicate
[377](https://docs.rs#377)//!
[378](https://docs.rs#378)//! In similar fashion it's possible to define custom validators, but a validation function receives a reference and returns `bool`.
[379](https://docs.rs#379)//! Think of it as a predicate.
[380](https://docs.rs#380)//!
[381](https://docs.rs#381)//! ```
[382](https://docs.rs#382)//! use nutype::nutype;
[383](https://docs.rs#383)//!
[384](https://docs.rs#384)//! #[nutype(validate(predicate = is_valid_name))]
[385](https://docs.rs#385)//! pub struct Name(String);
[386](https://docs.rs#386)//!
[387](https://docs.rs#387)//! fn is_valid_name(name: &str) -> bool {
[388](https://docs.rs#388)//!     // A fancy way to verify if the first character is uppercase
[389](https://docs.rs#389)//!     name.chars().next().map(char::is_uppercase).unwrap_or(false)
[390](https://docs.rs#390)//! }
[391](https://docs.rs#391)//!
[392](https://docs.rs#392)//! fn main() { }
[393](https://docs.rs#393)//! ```
[394](https://docs.rs#394)//!
[395](https://docs.rs#395)//! ## Custom validation with a custom error type
[396](https://docs.rs#396)//!
[397](https://docs.rs#397)//! To define your own error type and implement custom validation logic, you can combine the `with` and `error` attributes:
[398](https://docs.rs#398)//!
[399](https://docs.rs#399)//! ```
[400](https://docs.rs#400)//! # mod wrapper_module {
[401](https://docs.rs#401)//! use nutype::nutype;
[402](https://docs.rs#402)//!
[403](https://docs.rs#403)//! // Define a custom error type for validation failures.
[404](https://docs.rs#404)//! // Although it's best practice to implement `std::error::Error` for custom error types,
[405](https://docs.rs#405)//! // we are omitting that for simplicity here.
[406](https://docs.rs#406)//! #[derive(Debug, PartialEq)]
[407](https://docs.rs#407)//! enum NameError {
[408](https://docs.rs#408)//!     TooShort,
[409](https://docs.rs#409)//!     TooLong,
[410](https://docs.rs#410)//! }
[411](https://docs.rs#411)//!
[412](https://docs.rs#412)//! // Define a custom validation function for `Name`.
[413](https://docs.rs#413)//! // The function returns `Result<(), NameError>`, where `Ok(())` indicates a valid name,
[414](https://docs.rs#414)//! // and `Err(NameError)` represents a specific validation failure.
[415](https://docs.rs#415)//! fn validate_name(name: &str) -> Result<(), NameError> {
[416](https://docs.rs#416)//!     if name.len() < 3 {
[417](https://docs.rs#417)//!         Err(NameError::TooShort)
[418](https://docs.rs#418)//!     } else if name.len() > 10 {
[419](https://docs.rs#419)//!         Err(NameError::TooLong)
[420](https://docs.rs#420)//!     } else {
[421](https://docs.rs#421)//!         Ok(())
[422](https://docs.rs#422)//!     }
[423](https://docs.rs#423)//! }
[424](https://docs.rs#424)//!
[425](https://docs.rs#425)//! // Define a newtype `Name` with custom validation logic and custom error.
[426](https://docs.rs#426)//! #[nutype(
[427](https://docs.rs#427)//!     validate(with = validate_name, error = NameError),
[428](https://docs.rs#428)//!     derive(Debug, PartialEq),
[429](https://docs.rs#429)//! )]
[430](https://docs.rs#430)//! struct Name(String);
[431](https://docs.rs#431)//! # }
[432](https://docs.rs#432)//! ```
[433](https://docs.rs#433)//!
[434](https://docs.rs#434)//! It's important to ensure that the type specified in the `error` attribute matches the error type returned by the validation function.
[435](https://docs.rs#435)//!
[436](https://docs.rs#436)//!
[437](https://docs.rs#437)//! ## Deriving Traits
[438](https://docs.rs#438)//!
[439](https://docs.rs#439)//! There are two ways to derive traits for a `nutype`.
[440](https://docs.rs#440)//!
[441](https://docs.rs#441)//! ### `derive`
[442](https://docs.rs#442)//!
[443](https://docs.rs#443)//! The recommended approach is to use the `derive(..)` attribute within the `#[nutype(..)]` macro:
[444](https://docs.rs#444)//!
[445](https://docs.rs#445)//! ```rust
[446](https://docs.rs#446)//! use nutype::nutype;
[447](https://docs.rs#447)//!
[448](https://docs.rs#448)//! #[nutype(derive(Debug))]
[449](https://docs.rs#449)//! pub struct Username(String);
[450](https://docs.rs#450)//! ```
[451](https://docs.rs#451)//!
[452](https://docs.rs#452)//! When using `derive`, `nutype` ensures that the derived traits do not compromise the type's invariants (i.e., validation constraints).
[453](https://docs.rs#453)//!
[454](https://docs.rs#454)//! However, this approach has a limitation: only a predefined set of traits is supported. Deriving arbitrary third-party traits is not allowed via `derive`.
[455](https://docs.rs#455)//!
[456](https://docs.rs#456)//! ### `derive_unchecked`
[457](https://docs.rs#457)//!
[458](https://docs.rs#458)//! To overcome this limitation, you can use the `derive_unchecked(..)` attribute (requires the corresponding feature flag to be enabled):
[459](https://docs.rs#459)//!
[460](https://docs.rs#460)//! ```rust
[461](https://docs.rs#461)//! use nutype::nutype;
[462](https://docs.rs#462)//!
[463](https://docs.rs#463)//! #[nutype(derive_unchecked(std::fmt::Debug))]
[464](https://docs.rs#464)//! pub struct Username(String);
[465](https://docs.rs#465)//! ```
[466](https://docs.rs#466)//!
[467](https://docs.rs#467)//! This enables deriving arbitrary traits, including those from third-party crates.
[468](https://docs.rs#468)//! However, **use this with caution**: `nutype` cannot verify that these traits preserve the invariants of the type.
[469](https://docs.rs#469)//! It is the developer's responsibility to ensure that the derived traits do not introduce ways to bypass validation (e.g., by allowing mutable access to the inner value).
[470](https://docs.rs#470)//!
[471](https://docs.rs#471)//!
[472](https://docs.rs#472)//! ### `cfg_attr`
[473](https://docs.rs#473)//!
[474](https://docs.rs#474)//! You can use `cfg_attr` to conditionally derive traits based on `cfg` predicates:
[475](https://docs.rs#475)//!
[476](https://docs.rs#476)//! ```rust
[477](https://docs.rs#477)//! use nutype::nutype;
[478](https://docs.rs#478)//!
[479](https://docs.rs#479)//! #[nutype(
[480](https://docs.rs#480)//!     derive(Debug, PartialEq),
[481](https://docs.rs#481)//!     cfg_attr(test, derive(Clone)),
[482](https://docs.rs#482)//! )]
[483](https://docs.rs#483)//! pub struct Email(String);
[484](https://docs.rs#484)//! ```
[485](https://docs.rs#485)//!
[486](https://docs.rs#486)//! Only `derive(...)` and `derive_unchecked(...)` are supported inside `cfg_attr`.
[487](https://docs.rs#487)//!
[488](https://docs.rs#488)//! Complex predicates work as well:
[489](https://docs.rs#489)//!
[490](https://docs.rs#490)//! ```rust
[491](https://docs.rs#491)//! use nutype::nutype;
[492](https://docs.rs#492)//!
[493](https://docs.rs#493)//! #[nutype(
[494](https://docs.rs#494)//!     derive(Debug),
[495](https://docs.rs#495)//!     cfg_attr(all(test, debug_assertions), derive(Clone, Display)),
[496](https://docs.rs#496)//! )]
[497](https://docs.rs#497)//! pub struct Label(String);
[498](https://docs.rs#498)//! ```
[499](https://docs.rs#499)//!
[500](https://docs.rs#500)//! Multiple `cfg_attr` entries are allowed:
[501](https://docs.rs#501)//!
[502](https://docs.rs#502)//! ```rust
[503](https://docs.rs#503)//! use nutype::nutype;
[504](https://docs.rs#504)//!
[505](https://docs.rs#505)//! #[nutype(
[506](https://docs.rs#506)//!     derive(Debug),
[507](https://docs.rs#507)//!     cfg_attr(test, derive(Clone)),
[508](https://docs.rs#508)//!     cfg_attr(test, derive(Display)),
[509](https://docs.rs#509)//! )]
[510](https://docs.rs#510)//! pub struct Tag(String);
[511](https://docs.rs#511)//! ```
[512](https://docs.rs#512)//!
[513](https://docs.rs#513)//! Note that a trait cannot appear in both unconditional `derive` and `cfg_attr` `derive` at the same time.
[514](https://docs.rs#514)//!
[515](https://docs.rs#515)//!
[516](https://docs.rs#516)//! ## Constants
[517](https://docs.rs#517)//!
[518](https://docs.rs#518)//! You can mark a type with the `const_fn` flag. In that case, its `new` and `try_new` functions will be declared as `const`:
[519](https://docs.rs#519)//!
[520](https://docs.rs#520)//! ```
[521](https://docs.rs#521)//! use nutype::nutype;
[522](https://docs.rs#522)//!
[523](https://docs.rs#523)//! #[nutype(
[524](https://docs.rs#524)//!     const_fn,
[525](https://docs.rs#525)//!     derive(Debug),
[526](https://docs.rs#526)//!     validate(greater_or_equal = -273.15),
[527](https://docs.rs#527)//! )]
[528](https://docs.rs#528)//! pub struct Celsius(f64);
[529](https://docs.rs#529)//!
[530](https://docs.rs#530)//! // Since `Result::unwrap()` is not allowed in `const` contexts,
[531](https://docs.rs#531)//! // we must manually handle the `Result` when creating constants.
[532](https://docs.rs#532)//! // Any attempt to instantiate an invalid `Celsius` at compile time
[533](https://docs.rs#533)//! // will trigger a compilation error:
[534](https://docs.rs#534)//! const FREEZING_POINT: Celsius = match Celsius::try_new(0.0) {
[535](https://docs.rs#535)//!     Ok(value) => value,
[536](https://docs.rs#536)//!     Err(_) => panic!("Invalid value"),
[537](https://docs.rs#537)//! };
[538](https://docs.rs#538)//!
[539](https://docs.rs#539)//! assert_eq!(FREEZING_POINT.into_inner(), 0.0);
[540](https://docs.rs#540)//!
[541](https://docs.rs#541)//! // Alternatively, you can use a helper macro like this:
[542](https://docs.rs#542)//! macro_rules! nutype_const {
[543](https://docs.rs#543)//!     ($name:ident, $ty:ty, $value:expr) => {
[544](https://docs.rs#544)//!         const $name: $ty = match <$ty>::try_new($value) {
[545](https://docs.rs#545)//!             Ok(value) => value,
[546](https://docs.rs#546)//!             Err(_) => panic!("Invalid value"),
[547](https://docs.rs#547)//!         };
[548](https://docs.rs#548)//!     };
[549](https://docs.rs#549)//! }
[550](https://docs.rs#550)//!
[551](https://docs.rs#551)//! nutype_const!(WATER_BOILING_POINT, Celsius, 100.0);
[552](https://docs.rs#552)//!
[553](https://docs.rs#553)//! assert_eq!(WATER_BOILING_POINT.into_inner(), 100.0);
[554](https://docs.rs#554)//! ```
[555](https://docs.rs#555)//! Note that `const` works only for stack allocated types.
[556](https://docs.rs#556)//! If you are dealing with a heap allocated type (e.g. `String`) you should consider using `static` with [`LazyLock`](https://doc.rust-lang.org/beta/std/sync/struct.LazyLock.html).
[557](https://docs.rs#557)//!
[558](https://docs.rs#558)//! ## Recipes
[559](https://docs.rs#559)//!
[560](https://docs.rs#560)//! ### Obtaining a reference to the inner value
[561](https://docs.rs#561)//!
[562](https://docs.rs#562)//! The function `.into_inner()` takes ownership of the newtype and returns its inner type. However, if you only need to borrow the inner value (rather than consume it), you can derive `AsRef`. This allows you to call `as_ref()` to obtain a reference to the underlying data:
[563](https://docs.rs#563)//!
[564](https://docs.rs#564)//! ```rs
[565](https://docs.rs#565)//! use nutype::nutype;
[566](https://docs.rs#566)//!
[567](https://docs.rs#567)//! #[nutype(derive(AsRef))]
[568](https://docs.rs#568)//! struct Username(String);
[569](https://docs.rs#569)//!
[570](https://docs.rs#570)//! let username = Username::new("Jack");
[571](https://docs.rs#571)//! assert_eq!(username.as_ref(), "Jack");
[572](https://docs.rs#572)//! ```
[573](https://docs.rs#573)//!
[574](https://docs.rs#574)//! ### Derive `Default`
[575](https://docs.rs#575)//!
[576](https://docs.rs#576)//! ```
[577](https://docs.rs#577)//! use nutype::nutype;
[578](https://docs.rs#578)//!
[579](https://docs.rs#579)//! #[nutype(
[580](https://docs.rs#580)//!     derive(Default),
[581](https://docs.rs#581)//!     default = "Anonymous",
[582](https://docs.rs#582)//! )]
[583](https://docs.rs#583)//! pub struct Name(String);
[584](https://docs.rs#584)//! ```
[585](https://docs.rs#585)//!
[586](https://docs.rs#586)//! ### Derive `Eq` and `Ord` on float types
[587](https://docs.rs#587)//!
[588](https://docs.rs#588)//! With nutype it's possible to derive `Eq` and `Ord` if there is `finite` validation set.
[589](https://docs.rs#589)//! The `finite` validation ensures that the valid value excludes `NaN`.
[590](https://docs.rs#590)//!
[591](https://docs.rs#591)//! ```
[592](https://docs.rs#592)//! use nutype::nutype;
[593](https://docs.rs#593)//!
[594](https://docs.rs#594)//! #[nutype(
[595](https://docs.rs#595)//!     validate(finite),
[596](https://docs.rs#596)//!     derive(PartialEq, Eq, PartialOrd, Ord),
[597](https://docs.rs#597)//! )]
[598](https://docs.rs#598)//! pub struct Weight(f64);
[599](https://docs.rs#599)//! ```
[600](https://docs.rs#600)//!
[601](https://docs.rs#601)//! ## Constructor visibility
[602](https://docs.rs#602)//!
[603](https://docs.rs#603)//! By default, the constructor functions (`new()` or `try_new()`) are public.
[604](https://docs.rs#604)//! You can control their visibility using the `constructor(visibility = ...)` attribute:
[605](https://docs.rs#605)//!
[606](https://docs.rs#606)//! ```
[607](https://docs.rs#607)//! use nutype::nutype;
[608](https://docs.rs#608)//!
[609](https://docs.rs#609)//! mod inner {
[610](https://docs.rs#610)//!     use nutype::nutype;
[611](https://docs.rs#611)//!
[612](https://docs.rs#612)//!     // Private constructor - only accessible within this module
[613](https://docs.rs#613)//!     #[nutype(
[614](https://docs.rs#614)//!         sanitize(trim),
[615](https://docs.rs#615)//!         constructor(visibility = private),
[616](https://docs.rs#616)//!     )]
[617](https://docs.rs#617)//!     pub struct PrivateName(String);
[618](https://docs.rs#618)//!
[619](https://docs.rs#619)//!     pub fn create_name(s: impl Into<String>) -> PrivateName {
[620](https://docs.rs#620)//!         PrivateName::new(s.into())
[621](https://docs.rs#621)//!     }
[622](https://docs.rs#622)//! }
[623](https://docs.rs#623)//!
[624](https://docs.rs#624)//! // Can't call inner::PrivateName::new() directly from here,
[625](https://docs.rs#625)//! // but can use the factory function
[626](https://docs.rs#626)//! let name = inner::create_name("hello");
[627](https://docs.rs#627)//! ```
[628](https://docs.rs#628)//!
[629](https://docs.rs#629)//! Available visibility options:
[630](https://docs.rs#630)//! - `private` - Only accessible within the defining module
[631](https://docs.rs#631)//! - `pub(crate)` - Accessible within the current crate
[632](https://docs.rs#632)//! - `pub` - Public (default behavior)
[633](https://docs.rs#633)//!
[634](https://docs.rs#634)//! This is useful when you want to restrict where instances can be created,
[635](https://docs.rs#635)//! ensuring they only come from trusted factory functions or specific modules.
[636](https://docs.rs#636)//!
[637](https://docs.rs#637)//! ## How to break the constraints?
[638](https://docs.rs#638)//!
[639](https://docs.rs#639)//! It's discouraged, but it's possible to bypass the constraints by enabling `new_unchecked` crate feature and marking a type with `new_unchecked`:
[640](https://docs.rs#640)//!
[641](https://docs.rs#641)//! ```
[642](https://docs.rs#642)//! use nutype::nutype;
[643](https://docs.rs#643)//!
[644](https://docs.rs#644)//! #[nutype(
[645](https://docs.rs#645)//!     new_unchecked,
[646](https://docs.rs#646)//!     sanitize(trim),
[647](https://docs.rs#647)//!     validate(len_char_min = 8),
[648](https://docs.rs#648)//! )]
[649](https://docs.rs#649)//! pub struct Name(String);
[650](https://docs.rs#650)//!
[651](https://docs.rs#651)//! // Yes, you're forced to use `unsafe` here, so everyone will point fingers at YOU.
[652](https://docs.rs#652)//! let name = unsafe { Name::new_unchecked(" boo ".to_string()) };
[653](https://docs.rs#653)//!
[654](https://docs.rs#654)//! // `name` violates the sanitization and validation rules!!!
[655](https://docs.rs#655)//! assert_eq!(name.into_inner(), " boo ");
[656](https://docs.rs#656)//! ```
[657](https://docs.rs#657)//!
[658](https://docs.rs#658)//! ## Feature flags
[659](https://docs.rs#659)//!
[660](https://docs.rs#660)//! * `arbitrary` - enables derive of [`arbitrary::Arbitrary`](https://docs.rs/arbitrary/latest/arbitrary/trait.Arbitrary.html).
[661](https://docs.rs#661)//! * `derive_unchecked` - enables `derive_unchecked` attribute to derive any arbitrary trait.
[662](https://docs.rs#662)//! * `new_unchecked` - enables generation of unsafe `::new_unchecked()` function.
[663](https://docs.rs#663)//! * `regex` - allows to use `regex = ` validation on string-based types. Note: your crate also has to explicitly have `regex` within its dependencies.
[664](https://docs.rs#664)//! * `serde` - integrations with [`serde`](https://crates.io/crates/serde) crate. Allows to derive `Serialize` and `Deserialize` traits.
[665](https://docs.rs#665)//! * `schemars08` - allows to derive [`JsonSchema`](https://docs.rs/schemars/0.8.12/schemars/trait.JsonSchema.html) trait of [schemars](https://crates.io/crates/schemars) crate. Note that at the moment validation rules are not respected.
[666](https://docs.rs#666)//! * `std` - enabled by default. Use `default-features = false` to disable.
[667](https://docs.rs#667)//!

[687](https://docs.rs#687)pub use nutype_macros::nutype;
[688](https://docs.rs#688)
[689](https://docs.rs#689)#[cfg(test)]
[690](https://docs.rs#690)mod tests {
[691](https://docs.rs#691)    use super::*;
[692](https://docs.rs#692)

# clap - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/clap

## Expand description

Command Line Argument Parser for Rust

Quick Links:

- Derive [tutorial](https://docs.rs/_derive/_tutorial/index.html)and[reference](https://docs.rs/_derive/index.html)
- Builder [tutorial](https://docs.rs/_tutorial/index.html)and[reference](https://docs.rs/struct.Command.html)
- [Cookbook](https://docs.rs/_cookbook/index.html)
- [CLI Concepts](https://docs.rs/_concepts/index.html)
- [FAQ](https://docs.rs/_faq/index.html)
- [Discussions](https://github.com/clap-rs/clap/discussions)
- [CHANGELOG](https://github.com/clap-rs/clap/blob/v4.6.1/CHANGELOG.md)(includes major version migration guides)

[§](https://docs.rs#aspirations)Aspirations

- Out of the box, users get a polished CLI experience
- Including common argument behavior, help generation, suggested fixes for users, colored output, [shell completions](https://github.com/clap-rs/clap/tree/master/clap_complete), etc

- Including common argument behavior, help generation, suggested fixes for users, colored output,
- Flexible enough to port your existing CLI interface
- However, we won’t necessarily streamline support for each use case

- Reasonable parse performance
- Resilient maintainership, including
- Willing to break compatibility rather than batching up breaking changes in large releases
- Leverage feature flags to keep to one active branch
- Being under [WG-CLI](https://github.com/rust-cli/team/)to increase the bus factor

- We follow semver and will wait about 6-9 months between major breaking changes
- We will support the last two minor Rust releases (MSRV, currently 1.74)

While these aspirations can be at odds with fast build times and low binary
size, we will still strive to keep these reasonable for the flexibility you
get.  Check out the
[argparse-benchmarks](https://github.com/rust-cli/argparse-benchmarks-rs) for
CLI parsers optimized for other use cases.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

Run

`$ cargo add clap --features derive`*(See also  feature flag reference)*

Then define your CLI in `main.rs`:

```
use clap::Parser;
/// Simple program to greet a person
#[derive(Parser, Debug)]
#[command(version, about, long_about = None)]
struct Args {
    /// Name of the person to greet
    #[arg(short, long)]
    name: String,
    /// Number of times to greet
    #[arg(short, long, default_value_t = 1)]
    count: u8,
}
fn main() {
    let args = Args::parse();
    for _ in 0..args.count {
        println!("Hello {}!", args.name);
    }
}
```
And try it out:

```
$ demo --help
A simple to use, efficient, and full-featured Command Line Argument Parser
Usage: demo[EXE] [OPTIONS] --name <NAME>
Options:
  -n, --name <NAME>    Name of the person to greet
  -c, --count <COUNT>  Number of times to greet [default: 1]
  -h, --help           Print help
  -V, --version        Print version
$ demo --name Me
Hello Me!
```
*(version number and  .exe extension on windows replaced by placeholders)*

See also the derive [tutorial](https://docs.rs/_derive/_tutorial/index.html) and [reference](https://docs.rs/_derive/index.html)

# clap - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/clap/%7E2

## Expand description

`clap` is a simple-to-use, efficient, and full-featured library for parsing command line
arguments and subcommands when writing console/terminal applications.

`clap` is used to parse *and validate* the string of command line arguments provided by the user
at runtime. You provide the list of valid possibilities, and `clap` handles the rest. This means
you focus on your *applications* functionality, and less on the parsing and validating of
arguments.

`clap` also provides the traditional version and help switches (or flags) ‘for free’ meaning
automatically with no configuration. It does this by checking the list of valid possibilities you
supplied and adding only the ones you haven’t already defined. If you are using subcommands,
`clap` will also auto-generate a `help` subcommand for you in addition to the traditional flags.

Once `clap` parses the user provided string of arguments, it returns the matches along with any
applicable values. If the user made an error or typo, `clap` informs them of the mistake and
exits gracefully (or returns a `Result` type and allows you to perform any clean up prior to
exit). Because of this, you can make reasonable assumptions in your code about the validity of
the arguments.

The following examples show a quick example of some of the very basic functionality of `clap`.
For more advanced usage, such as requirements, conflicts, groups, multiple values and
occurrences see the [documentation](https://docs.rs/clap/), [examples/](https://github.com/clap-rs/clap/tree/v2.34.0/examples) directory of
this repository or the [video tutorials](https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLza5oFLQGTl2Z5T8g1pRkIynR3E0_pc7U).

**NOTE:** All of these examples are functionally the same, but show different styles in which to
use `clap`

The first example shows a method that allows more advanced configuration options (not shown in this small example), or even dynamically generating arguments when desired. The downside is it’s more verbose.

```
// (Full example with detailed comments in examples/01b_quick_example.rs)
//
// This example demonstrates clap's full 'builder pattern' style of creating arguments which is
// more verbose, but allows easier editing, and at times more advanced options, or the possibility
// to generate arguments dynamically.
extern crate clap;
use clap::{Arg, App, SubCommand};
fn main() {
    let matches = App::new("My Super Program")
                          .version("1.0")
                          .author("Kevin K. <kbknapp@gmail.com>")
                          .about("Does awesome things")
                          .arg(Arg::with_name("config")
                               .short("c")
                               .long("config")
                               .value_name("FILE")
                               .help("Sets a custom config file")
                               .takes_value(true))
                          .arg(Arg::with_name("INPUT")
                               .help("Sets the input file to use")
                               .required(true)
                               .index(1))
                          .arg(Arg::with_name("v")
                               .short("v")
                               .multiple(true)
                               .help("Sets the level of verbosity"))
                          .subcommand(SubCommand::with_name("test")
                                      .about("controls testing features")
                                      .version("1.3")
                                      .author("Someone E. <someone_else@other.com>")
                                      .arg(Arg::with_name("debug")
                                          .short("d")
                                          .help("print debug information verbosely")))
                          .get_matches();
    // Gets a value for config if supplied by user, or defaults to "default.conf"
    let config = matches.value_of("config").unwrap_or("default.conf");
    println!("Value for config: {}", config);
    // Calling .unwrap() is safe here because "INPUT" is required (if "INPUT" wasn't
    // required we could have used an 'if let' to conditionally get the value)
    println!("Using input file: {}", matches.value_of("INPUT").unwrap());
    // Vary the output based on how many times the user used the "verbose" flag
    // (i.e. 'myprog -v -v -v' or 'myprog -vvv' vs 'myprog -v'
    match matches.occurrences_of("v") {
        0 => println!("No verbose info"),
        1 => println!("Some verbose info"),
        2 => println!("Tons of verbose info"),
        3 | _ => println!("Don't be crazy"),
    }
    // You can handle information about subcommands by requesting their matches by name
    // (as below), requesting just the name used, or both at the same time
    if let Some(matches) = matches.subcommand_matches("test") {
        if matches.is_present("debug") {
            println!("Printing debug info...");
        } else {
            println!("Printing normally...");
        }
    }
    // more program logic goes here...
}
```
The next example shows a far less verbose method, but sacrifices some of the advanced
configuration options (not shown in this small example). This method also takes a *very* minor
runtime penalty.

```
// (Full example with detailed comments in examples/01a_quick_example.rs)
//
// This example demonstrates clap's "usage strings" method of creating arguments
// which is less verbose
extern crate clap;
use clap::{Arg, App, SubCommand};
fn main() {
    let matches = App::new("myapp")
                          .version("1.0")
                          .author("Kevin K. <kbknapp@gmail.com>")
                          .about("Does awesome things")
                          .args_from_usage(
                              "-c, --config=[FILE] 'Sets a custom config file'
                              <INPUT>              'Sets the input file to use'
                              -v...                'Sets the level of verbosity'")
                          .subcommand(SubCommand::with_name("test")
                                      .about("controls testing features")
                                      .version("1.3")
                                      .author("Someone E. <someone_else@other.com>")
                                      .arg_from_usage("-d, --debug 'Print debug information'"))
                          .get_matches();
    // Same as previous example...
}
```
This third method shows how you can use a YAML file to build your CLI and keep your Rust source tidy or support multiple localized translations by having different YAML files for each localization.

First, create the `cli.yml` file to hold your CLI options, but it could be called anything we
like:

```
name: myapp
version: "1.0"
author: Kevin K. <kbknapp@gmail.com>
about: Does awesome things
args:
    - config:
        short: c
        long: config
        value_name: FILE
        help: Sets a custom config file
        takes_value: true
    - INPUT:
        help: Sets the input file to use
        required: true
        index: 1
    - verbose:
        short: v
        multiple: true
        help: Sets the level of verbosity
subcommands:
    - test:
        about: controls testing features
        version: "1.3"
        author: Someone E. <someone_else@other.com>
        args:
            - debug:
                short: d
                help: print debug information
```
Since this feature requires additional dependencies that not everyone may want, it is *not*
compiled in by default and we need to enable a feature flag in Cargo.toml:

Simply change your `clap = "~2.27.0"` to `clap = {version = "~2.27.0", features = ["yaml"]}`.

At last we create our `main.rs` file just like we would have with the previous two examples:

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
// (Full example with detailed comments in examples/17_yaml.rs)
//
// This example demonstrates clap's building from YAML style of creating arguments which is far
// more clean, but takes a very small performance hit compared to the other two methods.
#[macro_use]
extern crate clap;
use clap::App;
fn main() {
    // The YAML file is found relative to the current file, similar to how modules are found
    let yaml = load_yaml!("cli.yml");
    let matches = App::from_yaml(yaml).get_matches();
    // Same as previous examples...
}
```
Finally there is a macro version, which is like a hybrid approach offering the speed of the builder pattern (the first example), but without all the verbosity.

```
#[macro_use]
extern crate clap;
fn main() {
    let matches = clap_app!(myapp =>
        (version: "1.0")
        (author: "Kevin K. <kbknapp@gmail.com>")
        (about: "Does awesome things")
        (@arg CONFIG: -c --config +takes_value "Sets a custom config file")
        (@arg INPUT: +required "Sets the input file to use")
        (@arg debug: -d ... "Sets the level of debugging information")
        (@subcommand test =>
            (about: "controls testing features")
            (version: "1.3")
            (author: "Someone E. <someone_else@other.com>")
            (@arg verbose: -v --verbose "Print test information verbosely")
        )
    ).get_matches();
    // Same as before...
}
```
If you were to compile any of the above programs and run them with the flag `--help` or `-h` (or
`help` subcommand, since we defined `test` as a subcommand) the following would be output

```
$ myprog --help
My Super Program 1.0
Kevin K. <kbknapp@gmail.com>
Does awesome things
USAGE:
    MyApp [FLAGS] [OPTIONS] <INPUT> [SUBCOMMAND]
FLAGS:
    -h, --help       Prints this message
    -v               Sets the level of verbosity
    -V, --version    Prints version information
OPTIONS:
    -c, --config <FILE>    Sets a custom config file
ARGS:
    INPUT    The input file to use
SUBCOMMANDS:
    help    Prints this message
    test    Controls testing features
```
**NOTE:** You could also run `myapp test --help` to see similar output and options for the
`test` subcommand.

There are a few goals of `clap` that I’d like to maintain throughout contributions. If your
proposed changes break, or go against any of these goals we’ll discuss the changes further
before merging (but will *not* be ignored, all contributes are welcome!). These are by no means
hard-and-fast rules, as I’m no expert and break them myself from time to time (even if by
mistake or ignorance).

- Remain backwards compatible when possible
- If backwards compatibility *must*be broken, use deprecation warnings if at all possible before removing legacy code - This does not apply for security concerns

- If backwards compatibility
- Parse arguments quickly
- Parsing of arguments shouldn’t slow down usage of the main program - This is also true of
generating help and usage information (although *slightly*less stringent, as the program is about to exit)

- Parsing of arguments shouldn’t slow down usage of the main program - This is also true of
generating help and usage information (although
- Try to be cognizant of memory usage
- Once parsing is complete, the memory footprint of `clap`should be low since the main program is the star of the show

- Once parsing is complete, the memory footprint of
- `panic!`on- *developer*error, exit gracefully on- *end-user*error

Because `clap` takes `SemVer` and compatibility seriously, this is the official policy regarding
breaking changes and previous versions of Rust.

`clap` will pin the minimum required version of Rust to the CI builds. Bumping the minimum
version of Rust is considered a minor breaking change, meaning *at a minimum* the minor version
of `clap` will be bumped.

In order to keep from being surprised by breaking changes, it is **highly** recommended to use
the `~major.minor.patch` style in your `Cargo.toml`:

```
[dependencies] clap = "~2.27.0"
```
This will cause *only* the patch version to be updated upon a `cargo update` call, and therefore
cannot break due to new features, or bumped minimum versions of Rust.

`clap` will officially support current stable Rust, minus two releases, but may work with prior
releases as well. For example, current stable Rust at the time of this writing is 1.21.0,
meaning `clap` is guaranteed to compile with 1.19.0 and beyond. At the 1.22.0 release, `clap`
will be guaranteed to compile with 1.20.0 and beyond, etc.

Upon bumping the minimum version of Rust (assuming it’s within the stable-2 range), it *must* be
clearly annotated in the `CHANGELOG.md`

`clap` is licensed under the MIT license. Please read the [LICENSE-MIT](https://github.com/clap-rs/clap/blob/v2.34.0/LICENSE-MIT) file in
this repository for more information.

# clap - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/clap/2.9.3

A simple to use, efficient, and full featured library for parsing command line arguments and subcommands when writing console, or terminal applications.

`clap` is used to parse *and validate* the string of command line arguments provided by the user at runtime. You provide the list of valid possibilities, and `clap` handles the rest. This means you focus on your *applications* functionality, and less on the parsing and validating of arguments.

`clap` also provides the traditional version and help switches (or flags) 'for free' meaning automatically with no configuration. It does this by checking list of valid possibilities you supplied and adding only the ones you haven't already defined. If you are using subcommands, `clap` will also auto-generate a `help` subcommand for you in addition to the traditional flags.

Once `clap` parses the user provided string of arguments, it returns the matches along with any applicable values. If the user made an error or typo, `clap` informs them of the mistake and exits gracefully (or returns a `Result` type and allows you to perform any clean up prior to exit). Because of this, you can make reasonable assumptions in your code about the validity of the arguments.

For a full FAQ and more in depth details, see [the wiki page](https://github.com/kbknapp/clap-rs/wiki/FAQ)

First, let me say that these comparisons are highly subjective, and not meant in a critical or harsh manner. All the argument parsing libraries out there (to include `clap`) have their own strengths and weaknesses. Sometimes it just comes down to personal taste when all other factors are equal. When in doubt, try them all and pick one that you enjoy :) There's plenty of room in the Rust community for multiple implementations!

`getopts` is a very basic, fairly minimalist argument parsing library. This isn't a bad thing, sometimes you don't need tons of features, you just want to parse some simple arguments, and have some help text generated for you based on valid arguments you specify. The downside to this approach is that you must manually implement most of the common features (such as checking to display help messages, usage strings, etc.). If you want a highly custom argument parser, and don't mind writing the majority of the functionality yourself, `getopts` is an excellent base.

`getopts` also doesn't allocate much, or at all. This gives it a very small performance boost. Although, as you start implementing additional features, that boost quickly disappears.

Personally, I find many, many uses of `getopts` are manually implementing features that `clap` provides by default. Using `clap` simplifies your codebase allowing you to focus on your application, and not argument parsing.

I first want to say I'm a big a fan of BurntSushi's work, the creator of `Docopt.rs`. I aspire to produce the quality of libraries that this man does! When it comes to comparing these two libraries they are very different. `docopt` tasks you with writing a help message, and then it parsers that message for you to determine all valid arguments and their use. Some people LOVE this approach, others do not. If you're willing to write a detailed help message, it's nice that you can stick that in your program and have `docopt` do the rest. On the downside, it's far less flexible.

`docopt` is also excellent at translating arguments into Rust types automatically. There is even a syntax extension which will do all this for you, if you're willing to use a nightly compiler (use of a stable compiler requires you to somewhat manually translate from arguments to Rust types). To use BurntSushi's words, `docopt` is also a sort of black box. You get what you get, and it's hard to tweak implementation or customize the experience for your use case.

Because `docopt` is doing a ton of work to parse your help messages and determine what you were trying to communicate as valid arguments, it's also one of the more heavy weight parsers performance-wise. For most applications this isn't a concern and this isn't to say `docopt` is slow, in fact from it. This is just something to keep in mind while comparing.

`clap` is as fast, and as lightweight as possible while still giving all the features you'd expect from a modern argument parser. In fact, for the amount and type of features `clap` offers it remains about as fast as `getopts`. If you use `clap` when just need some simple arguments parsed, you'll find its a walk in the park. `clap` also makes it possible to represent extremely complex, and advanced requirements, without too much thought. `clap` aims to be intuitive, easy to use, and fully capable for wide variety use cases and needs.

The following examples show a quick example of some of the very basic functionality of `clap`. For more advanced usage, such as requirements, conflicts, groups, multiple values and occurrences see the [documentation](http://kbknapp.github.io/clap-rs/clap/index.html), [examples/](https://docs.rs/examples) directory of this repository or the [video tutorials](https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLza5oFLQGTl0Bc_EU_pBNcX-rhVqDTRxv) (which are quite outdated by now).

**NOTE:** All these examples are functionally the same, but show three different styles in which to use `clap`

The following example is show a method that allows more advanced configuration options (not shown in this small example), or even dynamically generating arguments when desired. The downside is it's more verbose.

// (Full example with detailed comments in examples/01b_quick_example.rs) // // This example demonstrates clap's full 'builder pattern' style of creating arguments which is // more verbose, but allows easier editing, and at times more advanced options, or the possibility // to generate arguments dynamically. extern crate clap; use clap::{Arg, App, SubCommand}; fn main() { let matches = App::new("My Super Program") .version("1.0") .author("Kevin K. <kbknapp@gmail.com>") .about("Does awesome things") .arg(Arg::with_name("config") .short("c") .long("config") .value_name("FILE") .help("Sets a custom config file") .takes_value(true)) .arg(Arg::with_name("INPUT") .help("Sets the input file to use") .required(true) .index(1)) .arg(Arg::with_name("v") .short("v") .multiple(true) .help("Sets the level of verbosity")) .subcommand(SubCommand::with_name("test") .about("controls testing features") .version("1.3") .author("Someone E. <someone_else@other.com>") .arg(Arg::with_name("debug") .short("d") .help("print debug information verbosely"))) .get_matches(); // Gets a value for config if supplied by user, or defaults to "default.conf" let config = matches.value_of("config").unwrap_or("default.conf"); println!("Value for config: {}", config); // Calling .unwrap() is safe here because "INPUT" is required (if "INPUT" wasn't // required we could have used an 'if let' to conditionally get the value) println!("Using input file: {}", matches.value_of("INPUT").unwrap()); // Vary the output based on how many times the user used the "verbose" flag // (i.e. 'myprog -v -v -v' or 'myprog -vvv' vs 'myprog -v' match matches.occurrences_of("v") { 0 => println!("No verbose info"), 1 => println!("Some verbose info"), 2 => println!("Tons of verbose info"), 3 | _ => println!("Don't be crazy"), } // You can handle information about subcommands by requesting their matches by name // (as below), requesting just the name used, or both at the same time if let Some(matches) = matches.subcommand_matches("test") { if matches.is_present("debug") { println!("Printing debug info..."); } else { println!("Printing normally..."); } } // more program logic goes here... }

The following example is functionally the same as the one above, but shows a far less verbose method but sacrifices some of the advanced configuration options (not shown in this small example).

// (Full example with detailed comments in examples/01a_quick_example.rs) // // This example demonstrates clap's "usage strings" method of creating arguments which is less // less verbose extern crate clap; use clap::{Arg, App, SubCommand}; fn main() { let matches = App::new("myapp") .version("1.0") .author("Kevin K. <kbknapp@gmail.com>") .about("Does awesome things") .args_from_usage( "-c, --config=[FILE] 'Sets a custom config file' <INPUT> 'Sets the input file to use' -v... 'Sets the level of verbosity'") .subcommand(SubCommand::with_name("test") .about("controls testing features") .version("1.3") .author("Someone E. <someone_else@other.com>") .arg_from_usage("-d, --debug 'Print debug information'")) .get_matches(); // Same as previous example... }

The following combines the previous two examples by using the less verbose `from_usage` methods and the performance of the Builder Pattern.

// (Full example with detailed comments in examples/01c_quick_example.rs) // Must be compiled with `--features unstable` // // This example demonstrates clap's "usage strings" method of creating arguments which is less // less verbose #[macro_use] extern crate clap; fn main() { let matches = clap_app!(myapp => (version: "1.0") (author: "Kevin K. <kbknapp@gmail.com>") (about: "Does awesome things") (@arg config: -c --config +takes_value "Sets a custom config file") (@arg INPUT: +required "Sets the input file to use") (@arg verbose: -v ... "Sets the level of verbosity") (@subcommand test => (about: "controls testing features") (version: "1.3") (author: "Someone E. <someone_else@other.com>") (@arg verbose: -d --debug "Print debug information") ) ).get_matches(); // Same as previous examples... }

This final method shows how you can use a YAML file to build your CLI and keep your Rust source tidy or support multiple localized translations by having different YAML files for each localization. First, create the `cli.yml` file to hold your CLI options, but it could be called anything we like (we'll use the same both examples above to keep it functionally equivalent):

```
name: myapp
version: 1.0
author: Kevin K. <kbknapp@gmail.com>
about: Does awesome things
args:
    - config:
        short: c
        long: config
        value_name: FILE
        help: Sets a custom config file
        takes_value: true
    - INPUT:
        help: Sets the input file to use
        required: true
        index: 1
    - verbose:
        short: v
        multiple: true
        help: Sets the level of verbosity
subcommands:
    - test:
        about: controls testing features
        version: 1.3
        author: Someone E. <someone_else@other.com>
        args:
            - debug:
                short: d
                help: print debug information
```
Now we create our `main.rs` file just like we would have with the previous two examples:

// (Full example with detailed comments in examples/17_yaml.rs) // // This example demonstrates clap's building from YAML style of creating arguments which is far // more clean, but takes a very small performance hit compared to the other two methods. #[macro_use] extern crate clap; use clap::App; fn main() { // The YAML file is found relative to the current file, similar to how modules are found let yaml = load_yaml!("cli.yml"); let matches = App::from_yaml(yaml).get_matches(); // Same as previous examples... }

**NOTE**: The YAML and macro builder options require adding a special `features` flag when compiling `clap` because they are not compiled by default. Simply change your `clap = "2"` to `clap = {version = "2", features = ["yaml"]}` for YAML, or `features = ["unstable"]` for the macro builder, in your `Cargo.toml`.

If you were to compile any of the above programs and run them with the flag `--help` or `-h` (or `help` subcommand, since we defined `test` as a subcommand) the following would be output

$ myprog --help My Super Program 1.0 Kevin K. <kbknapp@gmail.com> Does awesome things USAGE: MyApp [FLAGS] [OPTIONS] <INPUT> [SUBCOMMAND] FLAGS: -h, --help Prints this message -v Sets the level of verbosity -V, --version Prints version information OPTIONS: -c, --config <FILE> Sets a custom config file ARGS: INPUT The input file to use SUBCOMMANDS: help Prints this message test Controls testing features

**NOTE:** You could also run `myapp test --help` to see similar output and options for the `test` subcommand.

The following is a list of optional `clap` features:

- **"suggestions"**: Turns on the- `Did you mean '--myoption'?`feature for when users make typos.
- **"color"**: Turns on colored error messages. This feature only works on non-Windows OSs.
- **"lints"**: This is- **not**included by default and should only be used while developing to run basic lints against changes. This can only be used on Rust nightly.
- **"debug"**: This is- **not**included by default and should only be used while developing to display debugging information.
- **"yaml"**: This is- **not**included by default. Enables building CLIs from YAML documents.
- **"unstable"**: This is- **not**included by default. Enables unstable features, unstable refers to whether or not they may change, not performance stability.

You can find complete documentation on the [github-pages site](http://kbknapp.github.io/clap-rs/clap/index.html) for this project.

You can also find usage examples in the [examples/](https://docs.rs/examples) directory of this repo.

There's also the video tutorial series [Argument Parsing with Rust](https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLza5oFLQGTl0Bc_EU_pBNcX-rhVqDTRxv) that I've been working on.

*Note*: Two new videos have just been added ([08 From Usage](https://youtu.be/xc6VdedFrG0), and [09 Typed Values](https://youtu.be/mZn3C1DnD90)), if you're already familiar with `clap` but want to know more about these two details you can check out those videos without watching the previous few.

*Note*: Apologies for the resolution of the first video, it will be updated to a better resolution soon. The other videos have a proper resolution.

If contributing, you can run the tests as follows (assuming you're in the `clap-rs` directory)

$ cargo test && make -C clap-tests test $ cargo test --features yaml $ cargo build --features lints

`clap` is licensed under the MIT license. Please read the [LICENSE-MIT](https://docs.rs/LICENSE-MIT) file in this repository for more information.

# clap - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/clap/*

## Expand description

Command Line Argument Parser for Rust

Quick Links:

- Derive [tutorial](https://docs.rs/_derive/_tutorial/index.html)and[reference](https://docs.rs/_derive/index.html)
- Builder [tutorial](https://docs.rs/_tutorial/index.html)and[reference](https://docs.rs/struct.Command.html)
- [Cookbook](https://docs.rs/_cookbook/index.html)
- [CLI Concepts](https://docs.rs/_concepts/index.html)
- [FAQ](https://docs.rs/_faq/index.html)
- [Discussions](https://github.com/clap-rs/clap/discussions)
- [CHANGELOG](https://github.com/clap-rs/clap/blob/v4.6.1/CHANGELOG.md)(includes major version migration guides)

[§](https://docs.rs#aspirations)Aspirations

- Out of the box, users get a polished CLI experience
- Including common argument behavior, help generation, suggested fixes for users, colored output, [shell completions](https://github.com/clap-rs/clap/tree/master/clap_complete), etc

- Including common argument behavior, help generation, suggested fixes for users, colored output,
- Flexible enough to port your existing CLI interface
- However, we won’t necessarily streamline support for each use case

- Reasonable parse performance
- Resilient maintainership, including
- Willing to break compatibility rather than batching up breaking changes in large releases
- Leverage feature flags to keep to one active branch
- Being under [WG-CLI](https://github.com/rust-cli/team/)to increase the bus factor

- We follow semver and will wait about 6-9 months between major breaking changes
- We will support the last two minor Rust releases (MSRV, currently 1.74)

While these aspirations can be at odds with fast build times and low binary
size, we will still strive to keep these reasonable for the flexibility you
get.  Check out the
[argparse-benchmarks](https://github.com/rust-cli/argparse-benchmarks-rs) for
CLI parsers optimized for other use cases.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

Run

`$ cargo add clap --features derive`*(See also  feature flag reference)*

Then define your CLI in `main.rs`:

```
use clap::Parser;
/// Simple program to greet a person
#[derive(Parser, Debug)]
#[command(version, about, long_about = None)]
struct Args {
    /// Name of the person to greet
    #[arg(short, long)]
    name: String,
    /// Number of times to greet
    #[arg(short, long, default_value_t = 1)]
    count: u8,
}
fn main() {
    let args = Args::parse();
    for _ in 0..args.count {
        println!("Hello {}!", args.name);
    }
}
```
And try it out:

```
$ demo --help
A simple to use, efficient, and full-featured Command Line Argument Parser
Usage: demo[EXE] [OPTIONS] --name <NAME>
Options:
  -n, --name <NAME>    Name of the person to greet
  -c, --count <COUNT>  Number of times to greet [default: 1]
  -h, --help           Print help
  -V, --version        Print version
$ demo --name Me
Hello Me!
```
*(version number and  .exe extension on windows replaced by placeholders)*

See also the derive [tutorial](https://docs.rs/_derive/_tutorial/index.html) and [reference](https://docs.rs/_derive/index.html)

[§](https://docs.rs#related-projects)Related Projects

Augment clap:

- [wild](https://crates.io/crates/wild)for supporting wildcards (- `*`) on Windows like you do Linux
- [argfile](https://crates.io/crates/argfile)for loading additional arguments from a file (aka response files)
- [shadow-rs](https://crates.io/crates/shadow-rs)for generating- `Command::long_version`
- [clap_mangen](https://crates.io/crates/clap_mangen)for generating man page source (roff)
- [clap_complete](https://crates.io/crates/clap_complete)for shell completion support
- [clap-i18n-richformatter](https://crates.io/crates/clap-i18n-richformatter)for i18n support with- `clap::error::RichFormatter`

CLI Helpers

- [clio](https://crates.io/crates/clio)for reading/writing to files specified as arguments

# rustdoc_types - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/rustdoc-types/

## Expand description

Rustdoc’s JSON output interface

These types are the public API exposed through the `--output-format json` flag. The [ Crate](https://docs.rs/struct.Crate.html)
struct is the root of the JSON blob and all other items are contained within.

[§](https://docs.rs#feature-flags)Feature Flags

[§](https://docs.rs#rustc-hash)`rustc-hash`

We expose a `rustc-hash` feature, disabled by default. This feature switches the
[ std::collections::HashMap](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/collections/hash/map/struct.HashMap.html) for [

`rustc_hash::FxHashMap`] to improve the performance of said
`HashMap` in specific situations.`cargo-semver-checks` for example, saw a [-3% improvement](https://rust-lang.zulipchat.com/#narrow/channel/266220-t-rustdoc/topic/rustc-hash.20and.20performance.20of.20rustdoc-types/near/474855731) when benchmarking using the
`aws_sdk_ec2` JSON output (~500MB of JSON). As always, we recommend measuring the impact before
turning this feature on, as [ FxHashMap](https://crates.io/crates/rustc-hash) only concerns itself with hash speed, and may
increase the number of collisions.

[§](https://docs.rs#rkyv_0_8)`rkyv_0_8`

We expose a `rkyv_0_8` feature, disabled by default. When enabled, it derives `rkyv`’s
[ Archive](https://docs.rs/rkyv/0.8.15/rkyv/trait.Archive.html),

[and](https://docs.rs/rkyv/0.8.15/rkyv/trait.Serialize.html)

`Serialize`[traits for all types in this crate. Furthermore, it exposes the corresponding](https://docs.rs/rkyv/0.8.15/rkyv/trait.Deserialize.html)

`Deserialize``Archived*` types (e.g. `ArchivedId` for [).](https://docs.rs/struct.Id.html)

`Id``rkyv` lets you works with JSON output without paying the deserialization cost *upfront*,
thanks to [zero-copy deserialization](https://rkyv.org/zero-copy-deserialization.html).
You can perform various types of analyses on the `Archived*` version of the relevant types,
incurring the full deserialization cost only for the subset of items you actually need.
